[quote=yzakastan;61324205][b]January 18, 2028: Izmir the Great[/b]

Orhan Izmýr, the shah of 33 million people and a booming industry worth billions, and yet, he was perplexed. There had been whispers of a coup to the north by effeminate males; the jurists had begun to whisper about whether the prophet had given permission for them to exist, and the orthodox had threatened to convene in Rosenmarkke if the matter was not solved.

Yet Orhan did not think as they thought, in prophecy, or in canon; he thought as a businessman thinks, was it stable? Would it bring more money into Yzakastan? 

Moving from his desk where he was seated, his fingertips brushing the finely carved mahogany, he turned on the record player that sat next to the desk, a delicious sounding Makam began to play, the notes oozing out of the speakers like an enchanting melody.

Orhan began to dance to the music as he thought.  He would summon the speaker and prelate of the senate and the Chamber of the People.  Yes, that is what he would do, and they would chat over tea and biscuits about the situation in the North. 

Moving swiftly, he made haste and dialed the chief steward, calling him to summon the two men for a meeting that afternoon. Vyzmir would not stay silent if silence was dangerous; they knew what silence could do if left untended.

The palm garden of the presidential palace had been built in 1767 by the grand caliph Abdul Mehmed IV; its tiled walls shimmered slightly in the light of the stained glass dome that sat over the garden.

Now tell me Edis, how is the Senate seeing the matter in Alaqar? Began the shah as his two guests sat down in their wicker seats.

Edis, a thin and pale man with a sniffle, replied, The Senate bears no concern in particular. We are shocked and horrified by the sudden overthrow of the centuries-old monarchy of Alaqar, but our own republic was founded by revolution, he chuckled.

Yes, but the Islamic jurists are talking Edis, they are talking, and when the jurists begin talking, then we must take into account their opinionsafter all43% of our country is Islamic, replied the Prelate Cahit Alparslan, a fat and dumpy man, with a waggle of his finger.

I am concerned about the financial implications, gentlemen. Alaqar is a large nation in the sea of the Shamats, and we are reliant on the stability of the sea, maintained by Hydronia. The market this morning plummeted 400 points, which is the worst weve seen in two years.

You have a point there, your honour, replied Cahit, But economic stability is not the same as societal stability,

I would disagree, Cahit, the two are interlinked, replied the shah. What does the jurist want more than anything? He wants his community to be stable, and for Islam to be proselytized to all people, replied the shah.

Inshallah, may it be so, replied Cahit with a nod of agreement. 

The culture is changing, atheism is rising, replied Edis, We cannot take religion into account here. 

The shah and Cahit laughed, I do not think that is the case, maybe in the university and coffee houses, but I do not think so, said Cahit.

Now, back to realistic talk, how ought this to be handled, with care, no? said the shah, spreading his hands.

Yes, yes, I say, I say, replied Edis, We recognise their government, if and only if, they do not trespass on the right of religion, and if they adopt the tenets of Ivankulism! 

It was a peaceful overthrow, no? asked Cahit. I think this is reasonable, 

Are there any of these Işıltılı Zarafet in our nation, femboys as they are called online, now replied the shah.

I wouldnt know, I am sure if you scoured the depths of hell you would find them there, laughed Cahit. 

Psah, be better in your manners, chided Edis, Yes, I would believe so, ask the Eunuchs,

The shah thought for a moment and said, Perhaps we should? 

I was only joking, your honor, replied Edis with light panic.

As was I! laughed the shah, The orientation of the Işıltılı Zarafet in Alaqar matters not, only if they are stable! Glory to Yzak, Glory to the shah, replied the shah.

Glory to Yzak, Glory to the shah, intoned the others, rising.

Will you gentlemen see the chambers discuss this matter and hold a vote? I want this solved by the end of the month, said the Shah. 

The other two nodded and left.

And Her Mother before Her: A Story from the River Sunthorn (1476)

Frya loved to run in the fields of flowers that surrounded the places she stayed with her mother and her brothers. They would spend winters near the base of the the mountains, and summers in the valley. Her mother would say twice a year, the air has turned, we need to go. Her brothers, Aermot and Castwin, would lead their goats and sheep. Frya would ride Hrianmoor, her mothers buck, until she was about 12. Her 13th summer they didnt travel back to the mountains. Hrianmoor wasnt walking like he used to, so they stayed by the river to see him off.
The morning he didnt wake up, her mom and the boys built a pile of wood and laid him atop it. Her mother threw carved pieces of bark around him, and she spoke over another, starting a small flame that erupted into a blaze. Frya had never understood how these strips of bark could make fires when spoken to, or leave flowers behind when burned. So she decided to ask, while they were watching Hrianmoor leave them on the smoke.
[i]Well, Frya, its something my mother taught me. Something she learned her mum, an she from her mum. I call it a family trick, but you must take care in who you speak about it with.[/i] She took a shred of bark that didnt make it to the fire. [i]You know what I told you about pictures, letters, and sigils?[/i]
Frya nodded excitedly, [i]Pictures are a way of saving what youre looking at, letters are a way of saving what you said, and sigils do the job of both![/i]
Her mom laughed, [i]Very good, love. I have sigils that I made, and that my mother taught me how to make. When I carve one into bark,[/i] she showed the girl the carved piece, [i] And burn it, the energy from the fire transforms the sign into something else.[/i]
She tossed the bark scrap into the flame. Frya asked what it said, and her mom looked up into the dawn skyline. [i]A hundred lifetimes in flowers. Id like to think I could really plant a field that could last so long. That some daughter will ask in a distant time, Why are there always flowers there?, and some mother will start on a tale spun by her mother, and her mother before her.[/i]

And from a dark cell in the Palac Wilnietschie dungeon, Frya wished she never asked. Her family trick was about to cost her her life.
